respondent_comments.quote: Now that it seems the buildout of AI infrastructure globally is nearing real activation, products going into data centers are at full procurement and manufacturing ramp-up. Thus, demand for our semiconductor end products and connectivity (power, networking and photonics) is booming. Similarly, defense is at an all-time high, with most of our product orders going to these two industries. Order volumes for medical, industrial and consumer products are markedly lower.

Aerospace and defense demand continues to be strong and growing, based on business backlogs. Competing for scare supply — electronics, certain critical minerals and other categories — is challenging on-time fulfillment for our supply chains. This is expected to get worse with co-dependent sectors also remaining strong and restocking challenges for automotive electronics.

Continued tariffs on products utilized in our product lines are being monitored by the business, which is working to mitigate or limit tariff risk. Geopolitical risk, especially in the Middle East, pertaining to commodity and energy markets remains a concern. There has been some increased cost and transit time for rerouted shipments due to conflicts in the Red Sea, Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal.
Business is still solid; we will increase revenue by 3 percent to 5 percent. We are considering foreign steel purchases for early next year because domestic steel mills are getting greedy.

The pricing volatility and lead-time extensions in this market are arguably worse than the pandemic era. During COVID-19, we saw a surge of price hikes and inventory buy-ups, which caused constraints that eventually leveled out. We are seeing nothing but consistent upward trends for both pricing and lead times that show no signs of slowing down. Specifically, 5-percent to 25-percent price increases for printed circuit board assembly components and 15-percent to 45-percent increases for bare boards are negatively impacting customer demand outlook into next year. This isn’t sustainable.
Sales continue to slide despite increased discounts. Mounting cost pressures from all fronts.
Business is starting to pick up especially with smaller firms. Just hope it keeps improving.
Conditions are largely unchanged from last month. The exception is pricing, which continues to rise, driven mainly by fuel and labor costs. Demand remains stable.

Business is more robust than expected, considering some of the economic headwinds still plaguing the industry. Lumber supply is tighter, and freight rates and availability are challenges. Many of our builders are pushing back hard on price increases. However, the outlook is favorable for the remainder of 2026.

macro.narrative: The current macro backdrop of robust ISM manufacturing expansion, rising new orders, and a healthy yield curve signals strong end‑market demand for Woodward’s aerospace and industrial control solutions, especially as AI infrastructure and defense procurement ramp up.  This demand, coupled with sizable order backlogs, supports pricing power and revenue growth, but supply‑chain constraints and higher input costs from rare‑earth metals and forged components will pressure margins.  Simultaneously, the company’s aggressive capex plans for new facilities and automation investments will strain working capital and free cash flow, while the modestly upward‑sloping yield curve keeps financing costs relatively stable.

implications.why: Expanding ISM new orders and AI data‑center buildout boost demand for Woodward’s aerospace and industrial control products.
Strong aerospace and defense backlogs provide a reliable revenue pipeline and support future sales.
Supply‑chain disruptions and higher prices for castings, forgings, and rare‑earth metals increase production costs.
Capital expenditures for new facilities and automation are rising, tightening cash flow.
Higher capex and inventory buildup from expanding orders strain working‑capital balances.
An upward‑sloping yield curve modestly raises borrowing rates, but Woodward’s strong credit profile mitigates the impact.
